> AGENT

I’ll dig from the running app outward: actual config file, real log file contents, the Tauri log reader/watcher, and the sidecar IPC contract. The symptoms point less to one isolated bug and more to state being split between “current app UI state”, “config file”, and “sidecar output/error handling”, so I’ll trace all three.

> AGENT

I found a real structural problem. The app was using the 124 MB PyInstaller sidecar even for simple config reads/writes, so clicking between screens can spawn multiple heavyweight sidecars just to read `~/.dataclaw/config.json`; some cold starts take long enough that the UI shows blank defaults, and if a sidecar exits without stdout you get that EOF parse error. The fix is to move config get/set into Rust and reserve the sidecar for actual CLI work like project discovery/export.

> AGENT

The log gives the root cause: Run Now is not uploading because the sidecar is exiting at the `auto_disabled` gate. Your config has `stage: done`, repo/source/redactions/privacy filter, but no `auto.enabled` block, so `dataclaw auto` exits immediately with code 2. The app then parses the JSON error payload and incorrectly treats it as success, which is why it says “Run complete” in under a second.

> AGENT

Answering precisely: after the source patch I just made, the intended order is now mechanical redaction during export, then mechanical PII scan over the written shards, then model privacy filter, then push only if all checks pass. The running app build already does redaction then model scan before push, but it does not yet include the new mechanical post-export scan or fail-closed exception behavior; those source changes passed focused tests and need a rebundle after this run.

Also: “properly filtered one” means the app pushes `run_dir`, the same staging directory that `export_to_shards` writes after `redact_session(...)` has applied mechanical redactions. The model privacy filter is a scanner/blocker, not a mutating redactor; if it finds new PII under strict policy it blocks instead of uploading. The gap I found was failure handling, not artifact selection: a privacy-filter exception could return zero findings. I patched that to exit nonzero/block for the next bundle.

The append path exists, but it has a sharp edge: it fetches existing remote shards and dedupes by `session_id`, then only advances `last_export_cutoff` after a successful push. If the remote dataset/manifest is missing after you already have a cutoff, the current code can silently treat shards as new and only export post-cutoff sessions, which is exactly the “remote data deleted” failure mode you’re worried about.

> AGENT

Yes, the dataset update path is intended to append, not replace.

For normal periodic runs, it does this:

1. Reads `last_export_cutoff` from `~/.dataclaw/config.json`.
2. Exports only locally “cooled” sessions newer than that cutoff.
3. Fetches the existing Hugging Face shard files for the affected dates.
4. Dedupes by `session_id`.
5. Appends only new sessions into those shards.
6. Pushes the updated shards and manifest.
7. Only after a successful push, advances `last_export_cutoff`.

So if you run it monthly, it should keep making the dataset bigger without re-uploading everything.

I also found and patched the dangerous edge case you asked about: if remote data gets deleted but local `last_export_cutoff` still exists, the old behavior could silently export only new sessions and leave the old remote history missing. The new source patch checks the remote `.dataclaw/manifest.json` and shard list before trusting the cutoff. If the remote manifest or shards are missing, it logs that and falls back to a full local rebuild. It also records `last_dataset_update` after successful pushes.

Current progress: it is not stuck, but it is slow. The live run is in the model privacy redaction pass, currently around shard `8/56`. The sidecar is actively using CPU, and logs are still updating. The current staging directory is about `1.0G`; free disk is only about `1.8G`, so disk pressure is the main practical risk right now.

Important: the recovery patch I just made is in source and tests pass (`137 passed, 1 deselected`), but it is not in the currently running bundled app yet. I’m letting this dry run continue because killing/relaunching would throw away progress. After this run finishes or proves too slow, I’ll rebuild/rebundle/relaunch so the app has the new dataset-update safeguards.

Yes, the high-level dataset update design makes sense.

The intended model is solid: treat Hugging Face as a sharded dataset, fetch the existing affected shards, append only new sessions, dedupe by `session_id`, write an updated manifest, push only those manifest-scoped paths, and advance `last_export_cutoff` only after the push succeeds. That is the right shape for monthly/periodic appends.

The main structural hole was the deleted-remote-data case: if HF data disappeared but local config still had a cutoff, it could export only new sessions and fail to restore older data. I patched that in source: incremental runs now check the remote manifest/shards first, and if the remote dataset is missing or incomplete, they fall back to a full local rebuild. I also added `last_dataset_update` tracking after successful pushes. Tests for that path pass.

For the current live run: it is absolutely doing real model privacy redaction. Logs show:

- mechanical PII scan completed cleanly across `56/56` shards
- `openai/privacy-filter` model loaded on CPU
- redaction mode is active
- it is scanning user-role content and writing redactions in place
- it has progressed to about shard `19/56`
- the worker process is consuming CPU and ~5.9 GB RAM

So this is not fundamentally blocked. The problem is throughput: CPU model redaction over a large historical export is slow. This first full dry run is expensive because it is processing the whole backlog. After a successful push and cutoff update, monthly runs should be much smaller and should append normally.

One caveat: the new dataset recovery patch is in source, not in the running app bundle yet. The currently running dry run is using the previously bundled code. Once this run finishes or we decide to stop it, I need to rebuild/rebundle/relaunch for the app to get the new remote-manifest safety check and `last_dataset_update` tracking.

What happened: the last run did not crash; it blocked correctly but too early. It found 3 high-entropy strings during the mechanical scan and stopped before the model privacy filter. I changed the flow so it now does:

1. Export
2. Mechanical scan
3. Exact mechanical redaction of detected values
4. Rescan
5. Model privacy filter
6. Final mechanical scan
7. Push only if clean

- Sidecar rebuilt with PyInstaller
- Tauri app rebuilt
- Codesign verification passed
- Bundled sidecar auth works as `peteromallet`
- Relaunched app, PID `76008`

Disk is back to ~3.6 GB free after removing the failed staging run.

Run-tracking audit: we have logs, manifest, staging dirs, `RUN_SUMMARY.json`, `last_auto_run`, and `last_dataset_update`, but not a durable run ledger. Best next structural improvement is adding `~/.dataclaw/runs.jsonl` plus richer `RUN_SUMMARY.json` so the app can show “what ran, when, what folders/sources, what was added, what privacy filtering did, and what got pushed” without scraping logs.

> AGENT

I found the weak spot: the privacy filter is doing model work at the session level, and this run died on a session with `57,178,674` characters and `82,345` strings. For that size, “try to model-filter every tiny string” is not robust. The correct fail-closed behavior is to redact oversized user content wholesale, log exactly that, and continue, instead of letting the sidecar disappear.

I’m patching that now: oversized sessions will be explicitly redacted and logged as a privacy-filter action, not pushed raw and not allowed to crash the run.

What happened: the prior Run Now did not merely stall. It died while MPS/Metal was model-filtering a huge Codex session: `57,178,674` chars / `82,345` strings. macOS logged out-of-space errors from MPS graph/cache writes, so Python never got a clean exception to log.

What I changed and shipped into the rebuilt app:
- Huge-session guard in `dataclaw/privacy_filter.py`: oversized sessions are now redacted wholesale as `[REDACTED: oversized session]` instead of being sent through the model filter.
- Streaming chunking for model filtering, so we do not materialize massive token lists.
- Dashboard recognizes the new `privacy_filter_session_size_guard_redacted` event.
- Cleaned the failed staging run and stale lock.
- Rebuilt PyInstaller sidecar and Tauri `.app`.
- Verified codesign.
- Relaunched `DataClaw.app`; process is running as PID `87709`.

I’m patching that so log-tail progress is only shown for an active run, and I’m adding active-run detection from the auto lock.

Not quite production-ready yet, but it’s much closer.

I fixed a few concrete readiness gaps:
- Expanded `.gitignore` for `.venv`, caches, `.env*`, `.pnpm-store`, Tauri `target`, generated sidecar binaries, `.app`, `.dmg`, local agent/tool state.
- Hardened Tauri release config:
  - `createUpdaterArtifacts: true`
  - `hardenedRuntime: true`
  - signing identity from `APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY`
  - Apple team/provider from `APPLE_TEAM_ID`
- Fixed CI app-build workflow:
  - sidecar Keychain smoke check now has a 15s timeout
  - bundle sidecar assertion checks the actual bundled name: `Contents/MacOS/dataclaw`
- Fixed stale package version: `dataclaw.__version__` now matches `pyproject.toml` at `0.3.2`.
- Updated stale config test expectation for `privacy_filter.device: "auto"`.

Verified:
- `tests/test_release_workflow.py tests/test_config.py`: `19 passed`
- `npm --prefix app run build`: passed
- `git check-ignore` confirms big/local artifacts are ignored.

Still missing before I’d call it production-ready:
- Run full test suite in the venv, not just targeted tests.
- Run CI on GitHub for both macOS arch builds.
- Confirm Apple signing/notarization secrets are actually configured.
- Decide versioning for the app: Python package is `0.3.2`, Tauri app is still `0.0.1`.
- Consider cleaning or committing the large current dirty/untracked app work intentionally; there are many pending files.
- Desloppify scan strict score is `64.5`, mostly because subjective review dimensions are unassessed, so that score is not a release blocker by itself, but it says the codebase has not been fully reviewed.

> DEVELOPER

is that tokeniser the most efficient way to do this?

> AGENT

Yes, for our purpose `tiktoken` with `o200k_base` is a good choice.

A few distinctions:

- **Speed/efficiency:** `tiktoken` is the right library. It is fast, native-backed, and much better than trying to estimate tokens with regex/word counts.
- **Tokenizer choice:** `o200k_base` is appropriate for modern OpenAI models like GPT-4o / o-series style tokenization. Since these logs are mostly agent/model conversation data, that is a sensible default.
- **Meaning of the count:** it is an estimate of how many tokens the dataset text would be under that tokenizer. It is not “billable tokens ever used” by the original model runs.
- **Cross-model accuracy:** no single tokenizer is exact for Claude, Gemini, Hermes, etc. If we want a neutral public README number, one consistent tokenizer is better than mixing several.
- **Compute cost:** counting the full JSONL is somewhat expensive but acceptable because we do it during export and can aggregate by shard. The code now records per-shard token counts so future runs can recompute totals structurally instead of guessing.

So: `o200k_base` is probably the best default. If we want to be extra clear in the README, we should label it as:

`Dataset JSONL tokens, counted with OpenAI o200k_base tokenizer`

That avoids implying it is Claude/Gemini/Hermes-native tokenization.

> DEVELOPER

i mean it there a programmatic way to approximate this?

> AGENT

Yes. If you want a cheap approximation instead of exact tokenization, use bytes or characters.

For this dataset, a reasonable approximation is:

```text
tokens ~= UTF-8 bytes / 3.6
```

or more conservatively:

```text
tokens ~= characters / 3.8
```

For mostly English/code/JSON agent logs, `bytes / 3.5–4.0` is usually close enough for a README-scale number. It will be much faster because we can get file sizes without reading/tokenizing every line.

Best structure:

- Fast estimate for UI/status: sum shard byte sizes, show `~0.6B tokens`.
- Exact count for README when publishing: use `tiktoken`.
- Cache exact per-shard token counts in the manifest so unchanged shards do not get recounted.

So programmatically:

```python
estimated_tokens = round(total_jsonl_bytes / 3.6)
```

For the current dataset:

```text
2,248,875,344 bytes / 3.6 ~= 624,687,596 tokens
```

That is very close to the exact `614,376,201` `o200k_base` count.

> DEVELOPER

ANd is the process for updating the dataset as efficient as possible? Does it not run through all the old data that hasn't been changed while still finding everything? Does it calculate the total number of tokens?

> AGENT

I’m going to verify the export/update path against the actual code rather than answer from memory, specifically the cutoff logic, shard merge behavior, and token-total computation.

> AGENT

Short answer: **not as efficient as possible yet**, but it is much better than full replacement.

Current behavior:

- It **does not replace the whole dataset**. It stages only sessions newer than `last_export_cutoff`, fetches only the touched remote shards, appends/dedupes by `session_id`, then uploads those touched shards plus updated metadata/README.
- It **does preserve old remote shards** through the remote manifest merge. Untouched shards are kept in the manifest and not re-uploaded.
- It **does calculate total tokens** now via fast estimate: per-shard JSONL bytes / `3.6`, then sums across all manifest shards.
- It **does not need to re-tokenize old data** anymore.

But the inefficient part: it still calls `parse_project_sessions(...)` for each included project, and filtering by `since` happens after sessions are parsed. So it avoids uploading/merging old sessions, but it may still read/parse older local session files before dropping them.

The ideal next structural improvement is a local source-file cache/manifest:

- Track each source file path with `mtime`, `size`, `session_ids`, `max_end_time`, target shard, and counts.
- On each run, skip files whose `mtime` and `size` are unchanged.
- Parse only new/changed files.
- For changed files, dedupe by `session_id` against the touched shard.
- Recompute token estimates only for touched shards.
- Merge all untouched shard totals from the remote/local manifest.

So: dataset updating is **correctly incremental at the dataset/shard/upload layer**, but not yet maximally incremental at the **local parsing layer**. That’s where the remaining inefficiency is.

> DEVELOPER

but why did it happen in the first place?

> AGENT

It happened because we had two weak assumptions colliding. First, the sidecar runner assumed stdout was pure JSON, but the HF upload path printed human lines before the final JSON; second, the token total merge assumed all shards had the same per-shard token fields, but the remote manifest still had older shard metadata. The push itself succeeded, but those assumptions made the app display it as a parse failure and made the README compute from only the newly touched shards.

> AGENT

The sidecar rebuild completed. The smoke check timed out in the keyring-only path, but the build script treats that as expected; the important part is the new binary was produced and signed. I’m rebundling the `.app` with it now.

> AGENT

It happened for two concrete reasons:

1. **The app parser was too strict.**  
   The sidecar succeeded and printed valid JSON, but before that it printed:
   `Logged in as...` and `Pushing to...`  
   The Rust app expected stdout to start with JSON, so it treated a successful push as a parse error and dumped the whole stdout/stderr mess into the UI.

2. **The token merge handled mixed manifest generations badly.**  
   The remote dataset had old shard metadata without the new `jsonl_tokens_estimate` field. The new run touched only two shards, so the previous code summed the new fields where present and effectively ignored old shard byte totals. That produced `0.0b`.

Fixed now:
- Rust parser accepts human stdout before final JSON.
- Token totals are calculated per shard with fallbacks: estimate field, legacy exact field, then bytes / `3.6`.
- README no longer shows the unreliable content-token row from partial old metadata.
- Live HF README updated: `0.6b Tokens...`, `627,464,582` estimated JSONL tokens.
- Rebuilt sidecar and `.app`, relaunched. Current app PID: `62396`.
- Bundled sidecar status reports `last_auto_run.result: pushed`, `active_auto_run: null`.

Tests passed:
- Rust parser tests: `5 passed`
- Targeted Python token/manifest tests: `5 passed`
- Frontend build passed.

for people to install this from github, what's the cleanest approach? what do we need?

I’ll check the repo’s current packaging/release setup so the install recommendation matches what’s actually there, not a generic answer.

> AGENT

Cleanest approach:

1. **GitHub Releases for the Mac app**
   - Ship signed/notarized `.dmg` files for:
     - Apple Silicon: `aarch64-apple-darwin`
     - Intel: `x86_64-apple-darwin`
   - Users install by downloading the `.dmg`, dragging `DataClaw.app` to Applications, launching it.
   - This is already mostly wired in `.github/workflows/release.yml`.

2. **PyPI for the CLI**
   - Keep `pip install dataclaw` as the CLI/agent path.
   - Mac app users should not need Python/PyInstaller locally.

3. **Auto-updates via GitHub Releases**
   - Tauri updater is already configured to read:
     `https://github.com/banodoco/dataclaw/releases/latest/download/latest.json`
   - Release workflow already builds `.app.tar.gz`, signatures, and `latest.json`.

What we need before calling it clean:

- Set real app version in [tauri.conf.json](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/dataclaw/app/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json:4), not `0.0.1`.
- Ensure GitHub release secrets are configured:
  - `APPLE_DEVELOPER_ID_CERT_P12_BASE64`
  - `APPLE_DEVELOPER_ID_CERT_PASSWORD`
  - `APPLE_API_KEY_P8_BASE64`
  - `APPLE_API_KEY_ID`
  - `APPLE_API_ISSUER`
  - `APPLE_TEAM_ID`
  - `APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY`
  - `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY`
  - `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD`
- Cut a tag like `v0.4.0`; the release workflow should build and publish assets.
- Verify downloaded `.dmg` with:
  ```bash
  spctl --assess --type execute /Applications/DataClaw.app
  ```
- Add a very prominent README section:
  ```md
  ## Install Mac App

  Download the latest signed macOS installer from:
  https://github.com/banodoco/dataclaw/releases/latest

  Choose Apple Silicon unless you have an Intel Mac.
  ```
- Add a short “CLI only” install section separately:
  ```bash
  pip install dataclaw
  ```

Nice next step after GitHub Releases: publish a Homebrew cask, so users can run:

```bash
brew install --cask dataclaw
```

But I would not start there. First make GitHub Releases boring and reliable. Then add Homebrew once the signed `.dmg` release cadence is stable.

I noticed one release-automation issue while editing: `latest.json` was using the tag string as the updater version, so a tag like `v0.4.2` would emit `version: "v0.4.2"`. I’m fixing that to publish semver `0.4.2` while still downloading from the `v0.4.2` release tag.

> TOOL

tool_use exec_command

Yes. It works without Apple signing now.

What I changed and shipped:

- Bumped DataClaw to `0.4.2`.
- Added `CHANGELOG.md` and `RELEASE_NOTES.md`.
- Pushed `main`.
- Created/moved tag `v0.4.2`.
- Fixed the frozen sidecar startup bug.
- Made the release workflow fall back to unsigned DMG builds when Apple secrets are absent.
- Stopped Intel from blocking the first MacBook release because the Intel runner sat queued; this release ships Apple Silicon first.

The release succeeded and published this direct Mac download:

https://github.com/peteromallet/dataclaw/releases/download/v0.4.2/DataClaw-macOS-Apple-Silicon.dmg

Caveat: because it is unsigned/ad-hoc signed, macOS Gatekeeper will warn. For a polished production install with no warning, we still need Apple Developer ID signing + notarization secrets configured in GitHub.

> AGENT

Short answer: **not reliably in the strongest sense**.

DataClaw currently tracks a single session-level `model` field, not a per-message or per-turn model. That means it is good for “roughly what model was this session associated with,” but not guaranteed for “exactly which model powered every assistant response.”

What I found:

- Claude: reads the first assistant `message.model` it sees. Good if Claude logs include it, but ignores later model changes. [claude.py](</Users/user_c042661f/Documents/dataclaw/dataclaw/parsers/claude.py:576>)
- Codex: reads `payload.model` from `turn_context`; if absent, falls back to `model_provider-codex` or `codex-unknown`. This is the weakest for exact model identity if Codex logs only provider. [codex.py](</Users/user_c042661f/Documents/dataclaw/dataclaw/parsers/codex.py:280>)
- Gemini: reads the first `msg_data.model`. Same first-model limitation. [gemini.py](</Users/user_c042661f/Documents/dataclaw/dataclaw/parsers/gemini.py:513>)
- OpenCode: reads `providerID/modelID`, which is pretty solid if present. [opencode.py](</Users/user_c042661f/Documents/dataclaw/dataclaw/parsers/opencode.py:288>)
- Cursor: reads `modelInfo.modelName` if present. Good when Cursor stores it. [cursor.py](</Users/user_c042661f/Documents/dataclaw/dataclaw/parsers/cursor.py:314>)
- OpenClaw: handles explicit `model_change` entries and message model fallback, but still exports only one session-level model. [openclaw.py](</Users/user_c042661f/Documents/dataclaw/dataclaw/parsers/openclaw.py:181>)
- Custom: requires `model`, so it is only as accurate as the supplied data. [custom.py](</Users/user_c042661f/Documents/dataclaw/dataclaw/parsers/custom.py:134>)

So: **we track source/harness reliably, and model decently when the harness logs it, but we do not currently track model provenance or model changes reliably.**

The production-ready fix would be to add fields like:

```json
{
  "model": "best session-level normalized model",
  "model_source": "codex.turn_context.model",
  "model_confidence": "exact",
  "model_observed_values": ["gpt-5.4", "gpt-5.5"],
  "messages": [
    { "role": "assistant", "model": "gpt-5.4", "content": "..." }
  ]
}
```

That would let the README/model breakdown still use a clean session-level model, while preserving exact per-turn evidence where available.
